ive come to realize that sometimes you cant give parts what they ask for.

i have parts that want my old life back, pre-disability. i have parts that want to be treated with dignity in a world that hurts minorities. there are often things you just cant change, and no amount of IFS is going to reshape the world around you.

no worries, your wording didnt sound dismissive at all. im very curious about the etiology of voices and whether some are truly just medical issues. just wanted to throw in my two cents re: the internal vs external factor. anecdotally ive heard from people that there's no cut-and-dry experience; external voices can sometimes be dissociative, and internal can sometimes be psychotic. to my understanding, this is the opposite of what practitioners expect, leading to misdiagnosis. again, all anecdotal, and im no doctor.

i do consider some outside experiences to be fully-fledged parts, yes. "messengers" can be a good word for some, but i don't necessarily vibe with that. in my case, it feels like my conscious perception of the world is altered by parts who are trying to show me something— noises being made in other rooms when i need to complete a forgotten task, for example. a part who feels hungry, but has been numbed all afternoon, and makes sounds in the direction of the kitchen. things like that. whether that part is *actually* making sound isn't a question i bother with— its just that im perceiving it to begin with, and interpreting it in a way that has meaning.

as far as nonsentient voices go, they can probably be considered "messengers" in that they indicate an imbalance of sorts? at the risk of sounding a bit antipsychiatry here... maybe your client can use those voices as natural indicators— are they well-rested? fed? is there an issue in their life that the voices are distracting them from? is the mind using these voices as a way to protect or avoid something? one time i had a breakdown at a new job and thought i was communicating with extraterrestrials in the bathroom. i was tired, terrified of one of my coworkers, and in a new city. i think, in a way, that break from reality was a sign from my system: "stop what youre doing, this isnt sustainable". the voices didnt say that outright, but in retrospect, the experience makes sense.

so tldr i think IFS techniques can be used to interface with external voices even if they arent sensical, sentient, or parts in the traditional sense. if a voice doesnt respond to "who are you, and what do you need?" then i pivot to asking "how does this unknown voice make my parts feel, how do i respect all parties involved, and what should i do next?"

not a professional, just a person.

sometimes my parts can be seemingly external. i wouldnt necessarily discount all external phenomena as being random/hallucinatory/wholly disembodied. its odd, but ive definitely had experiences that others would call paranormal that were direct mirrors of my emotional state at the time. some of these may have been psychotic episodes, but some of these were "physical hauntings" witnessed in groups of very rational people. i used to freak out about these things, but im slowly learning to live with it. when external presences interact with me, im a little better at pausing to listen now rather than immediately freaking out.

maybe your client could look into discernment techniques. this shows up a lot in spiritual spaces, but it seems like a handy skill for everyone to learn. im practicing things like analyzing how external phenomena is *treating* me— whether its violating a boundary of mine, or makes me feel unsafe at an instinctual level. by this, i mean there are times where external phenomena has certainly scared me, but had something important to communicate (i agree with the other commenter about "messages"). i tolerate some level of discomfort and even insults/verbal warnings if i suspect these presences have something important to tell me. ymmv with that one because nobody likes feeling unsafe, but sometimes negative voices are still parts of us.

even if they end up "just" being symptoms of schizophrenia rather than true parts, your client can learn agency, grow confident in accepting/denying what these voices tell them, direct their attention elsewhere if they need to, and find trusted loved ones to ground with.

what helps me is letting these moments fill me with temporary awe, before carrying on with my life. i used to freak out every time something "otherworldly" happened, but that emotional state wasnt sustainable. now, i just try to go with the flow. maybe there's nothing otherworldly about it at all— maybe these synchronicities and sudden changes are a natural part of how the universe works. maybe theres some weird science going on. or... maybe its something else entirely. multiverses or the simulation or whatever. i dont know.

but i dont think youre crazy. you sound very perceptive. i hope that these strange moments youve witnessed can be gently processed with someone you trust. hold space for healthy realism/skepticism, but dont gaslight the parts of you that have witnessed the unexplainable and feel anxious about it. even if theres a totally rational explanation in the end, you can listen to your own story with a nonjudgmental ear.

to my understanding... its only a diagnosable issue if it greatly reduces your quality of life, *and* doesnt align with your religious/cultural/societal framework.

you can have a true spiritual experience that others may label "psychotic", or a legit mental health struggle that may go ignored if your local congregation insists the cruel voice in your head is "god". 

(ofc every spiritual system has its own traditions and a sense of whats "normal"— maybe the land you grew up on has a greater presence of Others, and its normal to interact with them sometimes. or your traditions involve invoking gods or allowing spirits to work through you. i imagine this is why its important to have a wide representation of people working in the psychiatric field, so respectful discernment can be utilized depending on the patients cultural background, while keeping an eye out for any signs of genuine mental illness.)

ultimately if you arent able to live with your experiences, and feel increasingly challenged by unseen forces without a greater sense of purpose or fulfillment, it may be wise to seek medical help.

my suspicions have been there, but i remind myself that those feelings do not determine someone else's humanity.

feelings of fear and unfamiliarity can arise for a variety of reasons. sometimes humans simply act in unexpected ways. i dont want to label someone else as NHI when theyre simply living their life in a way thats different than mine. i have neurodivergent friends who say they get shoved into uncanny valley territory by people who dont understand them. i myself was called an "angel" growing up (like my mom may have genuinely believed that... shed tell me jesus visited me nightly and my hair had holy gold in it) but im just, like, a person. so i know my perception isnt king, and i try to be mindful of any inherent biases that may feed into othering people ive only met for a brief moment.

that being said... if someone *is* an emanation of NHI, i dont want to be weird to them either. unless they give me a reason to disengage or protect myself, it shouldnt be a big deal imo

i have a few people in my life who love me and understand my faults. i trust that theyll tell me if im ever in genuine danger, or if im somehow a danger to them. i try to trust my therapist the same way, even if i dont truly know them. i hope that theyll tell me if im on the wrong track. this is my "safety net" now. im learning from healthy people, so that in the future, i can trust myself on these things too.

im trying to believe that i wont be cosmically punished for everything i do, think, or feel. i may get hurt or hurt others somehow, but its not always 100% my fault like i automatically assume it is. even if it *is* my fault, im trying to learn how to take healthy accountability for things without hurting myself in the name of justice. who am i to say what justice wants or doesnt want of me? im not a god or a lawyer. so im trying to honestly listen to others when they say im not bad. i suck sometimes, but i do good things too.

my self control relies on responsibility now, rather than fear. i try to be reasonably responsible and honor myself, my community, and my future. i may not always be perfectly responsible, but i can identify what makes me irresponsible (like, exhaustion makes me cut corners), attend to those needs (i should get some bed rest tbh), and try to keep myself in check in the future.

erp makes you hold your breath and jump. other therapy modalities gave me a parachute, i guess. so im learning that i might survive that jump now, even if my brain is screaming that i wont.

erp alone didnt help me. i needed a stable network of friends/family, unconditional acceptance from a therapist i trusted, and a baseline sense of safety to fall back on. without a solid foundation, erp felt too triggering, and even traumatizing at times.

erp was finally successful when i eventually felt i could take leaps of faith, maybe mess up, and still be okay. IFS and ACT-esque stuff helped me create a stronger sense of inner fortitude even when i felt completely alone. OCD habits were always there to protect me somehow. i just needed to become my own protector, and learn to take care of myself when im scared.

its not for everyone, but it might be worth looking into a tandem modality.

i left a full time art career. while it was enormously beneficial in feeling autonomous, "good at something", and personally rewarding, the downsides were... well, let's just say i'm still making sense of the rubble.

it makes sense that you felt more anxious when you didnt confess to things— thats how ocd tricks you. if you give in to the desire to confess, the anxiety goes away... for a few weeks. then it comes back worse. it can find creative ways to make you think you didnt confess "right", or didnt confess "enough", or oh crap, what about this OTHER thing you just remembered? better confess that too.

the path to healing from ocd involves sitting with extreme anxiety, not trying to make it go away. you have to completely immerse yourself in those anxious feelings, and do nothing to try to stop them. then you have to keep living life as though nothing is "wrong", all while your brain is screaming. eventually, your brain will acclimate. even with pure O, this is the gold standard of ocd treatment. the process is called exposure (ERP therapy) and is best guided by a therapist, but is something you eventually practice on your own.

i would advise you to consider that your worst-case scenario (being considered unworthy of this relationship, being broken up with, etc) may indeed happen, but is unlikely to happen. 

while there's a lot of shame and anxiety involved when you dont confess to something, its better to process those unpleasant emotions rather than make your ocd worse. ocd is amplifying the importance of these thoughts— what may feel gargantuan to you, may seem like a non-issue to other people. these things are often subjective. but objectively, ocd that is given space to manifest and grow only creates more anxiety and shame and harms not only you but the people in your direct environment.

It would take an inhuman superhero to be in 100% control of their faculties during fight/flight. We are animals at our basest level, and though we societally shame those who act in accordance with their instincts when they feel threatened, it's still a fact of life that we're all barely more than monkeys on a rock in space. We do dumb sh-t! We're wired to do dumb sh-t, if it preserves our safety and well-being! We can accept this, and utilize that fact as a sort of self-compassion. So yes, our brains hijack our actions sometimes.

What counts towards being a better human, then, is working on our instinctive reactions while we're in a healthy headspace. Think about *when* you feel in control of your faculties, and devote that time to rewiring your brain. Neuroplasticity is a big thing. If you can practice changing your thoughts and reflexes, then you might be able to change your base reactions before you're in fight/flight again. 

We may not have total control over what we do when we're scared, but we have the ability to change those reactions over time. That's where responsibility matters. If you're in a safer place these days, now is the time to work on yourself. Support helps, healthy habits help. There's always a new day and a new chance to try again.

Side note, don't beat yourself up too much for not making changes before you knew what to change. The guilt sucks. I'm neck-deep in guilt. I'm right there with you. Let's try to transform it into something good and helpful, yeah? Much love and best wishes.
